strengths: Clear and intuitive problem formulation with effective hill-climbing interpretation of diffusion sampling, well-motivated through comparisons with prior methods
Practical adaptive control mechanism that dynamically increases exploration depth only when needed, providing better computational efficiency (7.6× NFE) compared to fixed-depth alternatives
Comprehensive experimental validation including two benchmarks, four human-aligned metrics, thorough ablations, and compelling qualitative results demonstrating coherence and alignment improvements
Model-agnostic and training-free approach that requires no model retraining, making it broadly applicable across diffusion architectures
Demonstrated robustness to different reward models (Table 2) and smooth scaling with key hyperparameters (Figure 2)
Well-structured algorithm with clear notation and detailed pseudocode enabling reproducibility and understanding
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: core components (latent inversion, reward-guided search, backward exploration) exist in prior work; primary contribution is adaptive depth adjustment

Significant reward model bias: improvements on ImageReward metric (4×) vastly exceed reward-agnostic metrics like HPSv2 (0.6%), suggesting overfitting to the chosen guidance model rather than general quality improvement

Weak and ad-hoc detection criterion for local maxima: reward plateau detection (Eq. 6) lacks principled justification; 'Always' exploration actually outperforms reward-based detection (Table 2), questioning the effectiveness of the detection strategy

Limited evaluation scope: only text-to-image with Stable Diffusion 2.1 base model; no evaluation on other modalities (video, 3D) despite broad applicability claims; limited comparison with recent test-time scaling methods
Multiple hyperparameters with unclear guidelines: λ, δ, dmax, N, Nb require tuning; sensitivity shown in Figure 2 but generalization strategy is unclear
Absence of theoretical analysis: no formal justification for why deeper exploration escapes broad optima; no convergence guarantees or quality improvement bounds
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; ImageReward may not be freely available; some implementation details unclear (CFG modifications during exploration, batching strategy)
Limited technical analysis: no visualization of latent trajectories; missing failure case analysis; no breakdown by prompt complexity; no human evaluation; unclear frequency of deep rollbacks
Questionable assumptions: using clean image estimate x̂₀ as quality proxy is heuristic; discrete timestep sizes may not be optimal; reward stagnation may occur naturally in good solutions
Baseline comparison fairness: SOP baseline uses 5 candidates for NFE matching rather than recommended configuration, potentially underrepresenting competitive baselines

strengths: Clear intuitive motivation: The hill-climbing interpretation of diffusion sampling is well-presented, and Figure 1 effectively contrasts different exploration strategies.
Model-agnostic and practical: Ctrl-Z Sampling requires no model retraining and is compatible with existing diffusion frameworks, making it broadly deployable.
Comprehensive ablations: Thorough ablation studies on key hyperparameters (d_max, δ, reward model choice, exploration triggers) demonstrate careful experimental design.
Computational efficiency: Achieves comparable or better results than Search-over-Paths with lower overhead (7.6× vs 10× NFEs).
Multiple evaluation metrics: Uses four human-aligned metrics across two datasets, providing broader evidence than single-metric evaluation.
weaknesses: Critical circular evaluation bias: ImageReward is both the reward model guiding exploration and the primary evaluation metric. The substantial ImageReward improvements (0.776 vs 0.677) are expected when directly optimizing that metric. Independent metrics show only marginal gains (HPSv2: +0.26%, PickScore: +0.08%, AES: +0.17%) without statistical significance testing.

Limited novelty: Core components (backward inversion, reward-guided sampling) are well-established. Adaptive inversion depth—the main contribution—is a straightforward extension. The 'Always' ablation shows always exploring yields higher ImageReward (0.931 vs 0.776), suggesting adaptivity primarily improves efficiency, not algorithmic performance.

Weak theoretical justification: Local maxima detection via simple reward plateau checking (Eq. 6) lacks rigor. The early stopping criterion (t ≤ T-λ) and choice of λ=15 are justified informally without ablation. Why these parameters specifically is unclear.
Narrow experimental scope: Evaluated on only one model (Stable Diffusion 2.1), one task (text-to-image), and two datasets. Claims of 'broad applicability' across video, audio, 3D are unsupported.

Substantial computational overhead with unclear benefit: 7.6× increase in NFEs is significant, yet marginal improvements (<0.3% on independent metrics) raise questions about practical utility and cost-benefit trade-off.
Missing statistical analysis: No confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests despite small improvement margins that could be within noise.
Incomplete design justification: Why N=20 candidates? Why δ=0.01 as default when ablations show δ>0 underperforms? How is N_b chosen dynamically? These details are vague or contradictory.

Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned, ImageReward is external, implementation details are vague (e.g., x̂_0 estimation after backward steps). No random seed reporting or multiple-run statistics.

Limited failure analysis: The paper doesn't discuss when/why Ctrl-Z fails or explain why the 'Always' strategy outperforms reward-based triggering, suggesting the reward criterion is too conservative but this isn't analyzed.
Unfair baseline comparison: SOP's candidate budget (5) is set for NFE parity, but SOP's own hyperparameter space isn't explored, potentially disadvantaging it.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies the failure mode of diffusion models converging to locally plausible but globally inconsistent or conditionally misaligned outputs
Clear presentation with effective visualizations explaining the core concepts and comparisons with related methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (HPSv2, PickScore, ImageReward, AES), two benchmarks, appropriate baselines, and thorough ablation studies
Better computational efficiency than SOP baseline (7.6× vs 10× NFEs) while achieving superior results, demonstrating improved exploration efficiency
Principled design choices with good justification, including the early timestep window restriction and practical batched search strategy
Model-agnostic approach requiring no retraining, improving applicability to existing diffusion models
Consistent improvements across multiple evaluation metrics, suggesting robustness of the approach
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (noise inversion, reward-guided search, zigzag sampling) with adaptive exploration depth; the core insight of increasing exploration depth when shallow perturbations fail is relatively straightforward and incremental

Narrow evaluation scope: only text-to-image tested despite claims of broad applicability; only Stable Diffusion 2.1 base evaluated; no empirical support for 'model-agnostic' claims; modest dataset sizes (500, 200 prompts); no evaluation on other modalities mentioned in introduction

Heavy reward model dependency without thorough failure analysis: circular evaluation concern using ImageReward to guide toward preference metrics; significant performance variance across reward models; no systematic analysis of miscalibration or noisy signal robustness

Overly simplistic local maxima detection: criterion (Eq. 6) merely checks reward stagnation; no analysis of detection accuracy, false positives/negatives; arbitrary acceptance threshold δ; no principled distinction between plateau and normal fluctuations

Insufficient theoretical analysis: no formal characterization of when/why local optima are escaped; no definition of 'narrow' vs 'broad' maxima; no convergence guarantees; claims about deeper rollbacks lack rigorous support

Modest empirical improvements: gains sometimes small (e.g., HPSv2 0.2671→0.2678 on Pick-a-Pic); only automatic metrics used (vulnerable to shared biases); no human preference studies validating claimed improvements; inconsistent improvements on aesthetic score suggesting potential trade-offs

Missing critical implementation details: hyperparameter choices (N=20, λ=15, dmax=∞) lack justification; batched search strategy incompletely specified; no CFG scale sensitivity analysis; no code availability statement

Incomplete empirical analysis: no wall-clock timing comparisons (7.6× NFE is substantial); no failure case discussion; no reward trajectory visualizations; limited analysis of when deep rollbacks are triggered; no investigation of per-prompt performance variation

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of local optima in diffusion sampling; excellent intuitive explanation via hill-climbing analogy
Comprehensive experimental validation across three benchmarks with consistent improvements on four diverse metrics (HPS v2, AES, PickScore, IR)
Extensive and systematic ablation studies demonstrating the contribution of each component (exploration depth, candidate width, reward models, initiation criteria)
Strong qualitative results showing visibly improved semantic alignment and visual coherence compared to baselines across diverse image categories
Technically sound with clear mathematical formulation (Eqs. 1-6), well-specified algorithm, and detailed implementation information enabling reproducibility
Accessible presentation with effective visualizations, particularly Fig. 1 which provides excellent intuition for the method
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead (6.72× increase in NFE) is a significant practical limitation with insufficient guidance on deployment scenarios and quality-efficiency tradeoffs
Lack of theoretical justification for why controlled random zigzag is optimal; missing formal analysis of convergence, optimality, or conditions for local optima occurrence
Critical dependency on reward model quality and calibration with limited discussion of failure modes when models are miscalibrated; acceptance threshold δ requires manual tuning with unclear guidance
Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: some direct comparisons involve different computational budgets; ambiguous attribution between algorithmic quality and increased computation
Limited analysis of failure modes, scaling to higher resolutions/larger models, and generalization beyond text-to-image generation; primarily evaluated on Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple runs reported; unclear if results represent single evaluations
No code release mentioned and some hyperparameters may require dataset-specific tuning; candidate selection strategy and diversity mechanisms could be more precisely specified

strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifies real issues with local optima in conditional diffusion generation with intuitive hill-climbing framing
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive experiments on three benchmarks with multiple human-aligned metrics and systematic ablations
Detailed technical description: clear pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and thorough mathematical exposition of the approach
Consistent improvements: demonstrates improvements across different models and benchmarks, suggesting some robustness
Well-executed ablation studies: examines effects of key hyperparameters (exploration depth, width, threshold, initialization)
weaknesses: Critical computational overhead inadequately addressed: 6.72× increase in function evaluations is catastrophic for practical deployment; the trade-off between quality gain and efficiency cost is downplayed despite fundamental importance

Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (DDIM, latent inversion, reward models) without substantive new insights; backward exploration has been explored in prior work (SOP, Resampling); the 'zigzag' framing is conceptual repackaging rather than fundamental innovation

Marginal and potentially non-significant improvements: gains over best baseline (SOP) are often <0.5 HPS v2 points (e.g., 30.91 vs 30.81); no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests provided to establish reliability

Weak theoretical justification: hill-climbing analogy lacks rigorous foundation; causal link between controlling backward steps and avoiding local optima is asserted rather than proven; no theoretical analysis of convergence or optimality

Fundamental dependence on external reward models: method's effectiveness critically dependent on reward model quality and alignment, but robustness analysis is minimal; if reward model is misaligned, method actively degrades quality; Table 3 shows high sensitivity to reward model choice without adequate analysis

Crude and ad-hoc local maxima detection: simple threshold δ on reward decrease does not reliably identify true local optima (could indicate plateaus or valid alternatives); introduces additional hyperparameter requiring tuning without principled guidance

Scalability and generalization concerns: limited to text-to-image tasks; unclear how 6.72× overhead scales to higher resolutions or larger models; applicability to other modalities or diffusion variants unexplored
Hyperparameter proliferation: introduces multiple hyperparameters (δ, d_max, N, λ) without principled selection guidance; Figure 2 reveals high sensitivity suggesting brittleness

Incomplete experimental validation: missing wall-clock time comparisons, statistical significance testing, evaluation of failure modes, and systematic assessment of when method helps versus hurts; qualitative examples (Figures 3, 5) appear cherry-picked with subtle improvements

Fair comparison unclear: uncertain whether all baselines received equal optimization effort; some recent competing methods (Chung et al. 2024) cited but not directly compared; differences from SOP remain unexplained
